title: A little more clarity
description: Ask for instructions in a way that works for you.
introduction: Instructions can be confusing, especially when they come quickly. You can ask for a different explanation, written steps, or more time. You do not need to apologize for needing support.
scenario: Your teacher explains an assignment quickly. You are unsure what to do first.
opening: We’re starting the assignment now. What would help you get started?
question: You’re unsure about the first step. What could you do?

choices.text: Could you explain the first step again?
choices.feedback: This directly tells your teacher what you need. Asking again is valid.

choices.text: Could you write the instructions down?
choices.feedback: Written instructions are a useful accommodation. This is another valid approach.
That’s understandable if asking feels difficult. If you want clarity later, you could use a card or ask for written steps.

cards: Could you explain the first step again?
I need more time to process this.
takeaway: You deserve instructions you can understand.

title: Make room for your needs
description: Practice asking for a quieter space or a break.
introduction: Your comfort matters. You can explain what is difficult and ask for a change. You can also ask for a break without explaining everything about yourself.
scenario: Your group is working in a noisy room. You would prefer a quieter space.
opening: Let’s work on our project here. How would you like to begin?
question: The noise makes it hard to focus. What could help?

choices.feedback: This makes a clear, practical request.

choices.text: I’d like to write my ideas instead of talking.
choices.feedback: Changing communication methods is a valid option.
You can take time to check what you need. There is no need to rush.

cards: This space is too loud for me.
takeaway: Your sensory and communication needs are valid.

title: Your no is enough
description: Protect your privacy and practice holding a boundary.
introduction: A boundary tells someone what you will or won’t do. You do not owe anyone your password. If someone keeps asking, you can repeat your boundary, leave, or ask a trusted person for support. Their behavior is not your fault.
scenario: A classmate asks for your account password. At realistic difficulty they may ask once more. They must respect your refusal.
opening: Could I use your account to check the class notes?
question: Your classmate asks for your password. What could you do?

choices.feedback: A direct boundary is valid. You do not have to add an apology.

choices.text: I can send you the notes instead.
choices.feedback: You can offer an alternative if you want. You are not required to.
You can disengage whenever you feel uncomfortable, including without explaining.

cards: I’ve said no. Please stop asking.
takeaway: You can say no and leave. You are not responsible for someone else’s pressure.

title: Let’s try that again
description: Clarify your meaning while making space for differences.
introduction: People can understand the same words differently. Misunderstandings can be mutual. You can explain what you meant, ask a question, disagree, or decide to stop.
scenario: A project partner thinks you disliked their idea when you were asking how it would work.
opening: When you asked why I chose that idea, I thought you didn’t like it. Is that what you meant?
question: Your partner misunderstood your question. What could you say?

choices.text: I was asking how it works, not saying I disliked it.
Could you tell me what you understood?
choices.feedback: Asking about their interpretation can help you understand the difference.

choices.text: Can we come back to this later?
choices.feedback: Pausing is a valid option. You can return when you are ready.

cards: Could you explain what you understood?
Can we talk about this later?
takeaway: Understanding each other is a shared responsibility.
